title: Morning Recovery Review (More Labs): DHM Dose, Evidence, and Value
excerpt: An honest Morning Recovery review: how much DHM is in the More Labs drink, what the science behind it really shows, side effects, user sentiment, and how its value compares with plain DHM capsules.
metaDescription: Honest Morning Recovery review: More Labs' DHM dose, the real science behind it, side effects, user feedback, and value vs plain DHM capsules.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Morning Recovery from More Labs is a well-made, convenient drink that put DHM (dihydromyricetin, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism) in front of a lot of people who had never heard of it. It is not a miracle, and it is not a bargain. The drink delivers a modest amount of DHM alongside electrolytes, vitamins, and herbal extracts, and there is no published clinical trial of the finished product itself. If you like the ritual of a ready-to-drink bottle and don't mind the price, it's a reasonable choice. If you mainly want DHM, plain DHM capsules give you more of it for a fraction of the cost per night.

**The quick summary:** Good for convenience and hydration. Weak on value. Evidence is borrowed from DHM research in general, which is promising but still mostly from animal and lab studies. No product, including this one, lets you drink heavily without consequences.

> **This is not medical advice.** This review explains general research and product information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using Morning Recovery or any DHM supplement if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, take prescription medicines (especially sedatives, anti-seizure drugs, blood thinners, or anything processed heavily by the liver), or are under 21. If you drink heavily most days or find it hard to cut back, a hangover drink is not the right tool; a doctor or the SAMHSA helpline (1-800-662-4357 in the US, free and confidential) is.

We don't sell Morning Recovery and we have no affiliate relationship with More Labs. That matters because it means we have no reason to talk it up or down. Where we mention products we do link to, we'll say so plainly.

## What Morning Recovery Actually Is

Morning Recovery is a single-serving liquid drink, sold in small bottles of a few ounces, made by More Labs, a Los Angeles company. It launched in the late 2010s after a crowdfunding campaign and became one of the first widely marketed drinks in the US built around DHM. It's meant to be taken while drinking or before bed after a night out, not the next morning despite the name.

The brand has sold several versions over the years, including an original formula, a zero-sugar version, and related products under the More Labs name. Formulas for supplements like this change, so the details below describe the product as it has generally been labeled. Before you buy, read the label on the bottle in front of you, not a review written months earlier (including this one).

### How you're supposed to take it

The usual direction is to drink one bottle during or after drinking, ideally before you go to sleep. The thinking is that DHM needs to be in your system while your body is still processing alcohol. A drink taken at noon the next day, after the alcohol is gone, has much less to work with. This timing advice is the same for any DHM product, and you can read the reasoning in our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025).

## Ingredients: What's in the Bottle

Morning Recovery has generally been sold as a blend rather than a single active ingredient. The main components that have appeared on its labels fall into four groups.

1. **Hovenia dulcis extract (the DHM source).** Hovenia dulcis is the Oriental raisin tree. Its fruit and seeds have been used in traditional East Asian remedies for drinking for centuries, and it's one of the main natural sources of DHM. This is the headline ingredient.
2. **Milk thistle.** A long-used herbal supplement marketed for liver support. Its active compounds, together called silymarin, have been studied for liver conditions, with mixed results in people. There isn't good evidence that milk thistle prevents hangovers.
3. **Electrolytes.** Potassium and other minerals. Alcohol makes you urinate more, so adding fluid and minerals is sensible, though the amounts in a small bottle are modest compared with a dedicated rehydration drink.
4. **Vitamins.** B vitamins and sometimes vitamin C. Heavy drinking can lower some B vitamins over time, but there's little evidence that a single dose of vitamins changes how you feel the next morning.

Depending on the version, the formula has also included other botanical extracts, sweeteners, flavorings, and preservatives. The original formula contained sugar; the zero-sugar version swapped that for non-sugar sweeteners.

### The proprietary blend problem

The most important label detail is how the DHM is listed. Several versions of Morning Recovery have listed Hovenia dulcis or DHM inside a blend, or as an extract, rather than stating a clear number of milligrams of pure DHM. That matters because "500 mg of Hovenia dulcis extract" is not the same as "500 mg of DHM." An extract might be standardized to contain a certain percentage of DHM, or it might not say.

When a label gives you a clear DHM number, you can compare it with other products and with the doses used in research. When it doesn't, you can't. Independent reviewers have generally estimated that a bottle of Morning Recovery delivers a few hundred milligrams of DHM at most, which is noticeably less than the 300 mg to 1,000 mg per capsule found in many single-ingredient DHM products. We'd treat any specific number you see online with caution unless it comes straight from the current label.

## DHM Dose: How Morning Recovery Compares

There is no official recommended dose for DHM. It isn't a drug, and no regulator has set a dose for hangovers. What we have are the doses used in animal research, scaled up loosely to humans, and the doses manufacturers have settled on.

Most single-ingredient DHM products land somewhere between 300 mg and 1,000 mg per serving. Many people who use DHM regularly take a serving before or during drinking and another before bed, which can put a night's total at 600 mg to 2,000 mg. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people usually think about this by body weight and by how much they plan to drink, and why more isn't automatically better.

Against that range, Morning Recovery sits at the lower end, and because of the blend labeling it's hard to say exactly where. That doesn't mean it does nothing. It means that if you've tried Morning Recovery and felt little effect, the dose is a plausible reason, and trying a higher, clearly labeled DHM dose is a fairer test of whether DHM works for you.

## The Lab Heritage: What's Real and What's Marketing

Morning Recovery's marketing has leaned on science, and it's worth separating what that science actually is from how it's presented.

### The DHM research came from university labs, not from More Labs

The modern interest in DHM as an anti-hangover compound traces mostly to work from the lab of Jing Liang, a researcher who was at UCLA and later moved to the University of Southern California. The best-known paper is Shen and colleagues, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience* in 2012. In rats, DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal, and it appeared to work by counteracting alcohol's effects on GABA-A receptors, the brain receptors that alcohol acts on to make you feel relaxed and, at higher doses, sedated. Later work from the same group and others looked at DHM's effects on alcohol metabolism and liver health in animals.

This research is real and published in a respected journal. But it was done on DHM itself, mostly in rodents, and not on Morning Recovery. A brand drawing on that research is borrowing credibility from it. That's normal in the supplement world, but you should know the difference between "DHM has been studied" and "this drink has been tested."

### Where Charles Lieber fits in

You may see Morning Recovery or DHM discussed alongside the name of Charles Lieber, so it's worth explaining. Lieber was a physician and researcher, based for decades at the Bronx VA and Mount Sinai in New York, who did foundational work on how the liver handles alcohol. He helped show that alcohol itself, not just poor nutrition, damages the liver, and he described a second liver pathway for breaking down alcohol (the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system, which relies on an enzyme called CYP2E1) that ramps up in people who drink heavily. Much of what we know today about alcohol and the liver rests on work from his lab.

That heritage is real and important for alcohol science in general. We could not find evidence that Lieber or his lab developed, tested, or endorsed Morning Recovery, and he died in 2009, years before the product existed. If you see Lieber's name used to suggest a direct scientific lineage for any hangover drink, treat that as background science, not as proof that the product works. The honest version is this: Lieber's work explains why alcohol is hard on the liver, and Liang's work explains why DHM became interesting. Neither tested this bottle.

## Does Morning Recovery Work? What the Evidence Shows

This is the question everyone actually wants answered, so here's the plain version.

**For the finished product:** we're not aware of any published, peer-reviewed, placebo-controlled trial of Morning Recovery. The company has cited internal research and customer feedback over the years, but internal testing that hasn't been published can't be checked, and customer reviews can't separate the drink's effect from the placebo effect, from drinking water with it, or from simply having a lighter night.

**For DHM in general:** the evidence is promising but early. Animal studies, including the 2012 rat study above, show effects on intoxication, alcohol metabolism, and liver markers. Human research on DHM for hangovers is limited, small, and not yet strong enough to say how much benefit a typical person should expect. We go through those studies in detail in [Does DHM work? An honest look at the science](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025).

**For Hovenia dulcis:** there's a long history of traditional use and some research, largely from South Korea and other parts of East Asia, on Hovenia dulcis fruit extract and alcohol metabolism. Some small human studies have reported lower blood alcohol or hangover scores, but they're small, and products and doses vary a lot.

**For the other ingredients:** electrolytes and fluid help with the dehydration part of a hangover. Milk thistle and B vitamins have little evidence for hangover relief specifically.

Putting that together: Morning Recovery may help some people somewhat, mainly through whatever DHM it delivers and the fact that you're drinking a bottle of fluid before bed. It's reasonable to expect a smaller effect than a higher clearly-dosed DHM product, and it's unreasonable to expect it to cancel out a heavy night. If you want an approach that reliably works, the boring basics still matter most: drinking less, eating beforehand, alternating with water, and sleeping. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what actually moves the needle.

## Side Effects and Safety

Morning Recovery is generally well tolerated, and serious problems linked to it haven't been widely reported. That's not the same as being proven safe for everyone, so here's what to think about.

### Common, mild complaints

- **Stomach upset or nausea.** Some people find a concentrated, sweet drink hard to take after alcohol, especially on an empty stomach.
- **Taste.** The most common complaint in reviews. Many people describe it as medicinal or overly sweet.
- **Sugar.** The original formula contained sugar, which adds calories and isn't ideal if you're watching blood sugar. The zero-sugar version addresses this, but non-sugar sweeteners bother some stomachs.

### DHM safety in general

DHM has not been studied in long-term human safety trials. Short-term use at typical supplement doses hasn't raised major red flags in the published research, but the human data are thin. DHM may interact with medicines that are broken down by the liver, and because it acts on the same brain receptors as alcohol and sedatives, combining it with sleep medicines, benzodiazepines, or similar drugs is something to ask your doctor about. We cover the details in our [DHM safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-safety-complete-guide-2025) and our guide to [DHM and medication interactions](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

### Who should skip it or check first

- Anyone pregnant or breastfeeding (there's no safety data).
- People with liver or kidney disease.
- People taking prescription medicines, especially sedatives, anti-seizure drugs, blood thinners, or diabetes medicines.
- Anyone under the legal drinking age.
- Anyone planning to drive. No supplement lowers your blood alcohol enough to make driving safe, and DHM does not make you sober.

### The bigger safety point

A hangover is your body telling you it took on more alcohol than it could comfortably handle. A drink that softens the morning after can make it easier to drink more often or more heavily, which is the opposite of what your liver needs. Use any hangover product, including this one, as a backstop for occasional nights out, not as a license.

## What Users Say: A Fair Summary

Reading customer reviews across retailers and forums, the pattern is consistent enough to summarize without inventing numbers.

**People who like it** tend to say they wake up feeling clearer, less foggy, and less wiped out than usual, especially after moderate nights. They like that it's one bottle instead of a handful of pills, and some use it as a social thing to share with friends.

**People who don't** tend to make one of four points: it didn't seem to do anything, it helped after a few drinks but not after a big night, it tastes bad, or it's too expensive to use regularly. A smaller group mentions stomach upset.

That split is what you'd expect from a product with a modest dose of an ingredient that has early-stage evidence. Results depend heavily on how much you drank, whether you ate, how well you slept, and expectations. Reviews are useful for taste and convenience, less useful for judging whether it works.

## Pros and Cons

**Pros**

- Convenient, ready to drink, no pills to swallow.
- Adds fluid and some electrolytes before bed, which helps on its own.
- Built around DHM, the most studied anti-hangover compound in the supplement space.
- Zero-sugar version available.
- Widely sold, so it's easy to find in stores.

**Cons**

- No published clinical trial of the product itself.
- DHM dose is modest and, on many versions, not clearly stated.
- Expensive per night compared with DHM capsules.
- Taste is a frequent complaint.
- Includes ingredients (milk thistle, vitamins) with little hangover evidence.
- Marketing borrows credibility from research that wasn't done on this drink.

## Morning Recovery vs Plain DHM: The Value Math

This is where Morning Recovery struggles most. Prices change and vary by retailer and pack size, so check the current price yourself, but the comparison works like this.

Morning Recovery is sold by the bottle, usually in multipacks. Historically, the per-bottle price in multipacks has generally landed in the range of several dollars per bottle, and one bottle is one night's serving.

A plain DHM capsule product works out very differently. As one example, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) (an Amazon affiliate link; we earn a small commission if you buy) lists 1,000 mg of DHM per serving at roughly $0.80 per serving at the time of writing. Toniiq Ease is another single-ingredient option, with 300 mg per capsule.

To compare fairly, compare cost per milligram of DHM, not cost per serving:

1. Find the price of one serving (one bottle of Morning Recovery, or one serving of capsules).
2. Find the DHM in that serving. If the label only lists an extract or a blend, you can't calculate this, which is itself useful information.
3. Divide price by DHM milligrams.

On any reasonable estimate of Morning Recovery's DHM content, plain DHM capsules come out several times cheaper per milligram, often by a wide margin. You can then add your own electrolytes for very little money: a glass of water and a pinch of salt, an oral rehydration packet, or a sports drink.

What you're paying for with Morning Recovery is convenience, flavor (if you like it), and the all-in-one format. Those are legitimate things to pay for. Just make it a deliberate choice rather than assuming the price reflects a stronger product.

## How It Compares With Other Hangover Products

Morning Recovery sits in a crowded category. Here's how it lines up with the products people most often compare it with.

- **Flyby Recovery** is a capsule blend that combines DHM with other ingredients like milk thistle, prickly pear, and electrolytes. It's often cheaper per night than a drink. See our [Flyby Recovery review](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025).
- **No Days Wasted** is a DHM product that lists a clear 1,000 mg DHM dose alongside L-cysteine and other ingredients. See our [No Days Wasted review](/never-hungover/no-days-wasted-dhm-review-analysis), and our head-to-head [Flyby vs No Days Wasted comparison](/never-hungover/flyby-vs-no-days-wasted-complete-comparison-2025) if you're choosing between those two.
- **Cheers Restore** is another DHM-based capsule product. Our [Cheers Restore review](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review) covers it in detail.
- **ZBiotics** works differently. It's a genetically engineered probiotic designed to break down acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol, in the gut, and contains no DHM. See our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) and our [DHM vs ZBiotics comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics).
- **Other recovery drinks** like rehydration beverages focus on fluid and electrolytes rather than DHM. Our roundup of [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares that category.

If you're deciding between a drink and capsules, the trade-off is mostly convenience versus dose and cost. Drinks are easier to take on a night out. Capsules usually give you more DHM for less money and let you adjust the dose.

## Who Morning Recovery Is Best For

**It's a reasonable pick if:**

- You drink occasionally and want something simple to take before bed.
- You strongly prefer drinking something over swallowing pills.
- You want to share something with a group on a night out.
- Cost per night isn't a major concern.

**You'll probably do better with something else if:**

- You want a clear, known DHM dose so you can judge whether DHM works for you.
- You're price-sensitive or drink more than occasionally.
- You've tried Morning Recovery and felt little effect. A clearly labeled 300 mg to 1,000 mg DHM product is a fairer test.
- You need something that will let you drive or work safely after drinking. Nothing does that.

## Our Bottom Line

Morning Recovery deserves credit for bringing DHM into the mainstream and for being an easy, pleasant-enough way to add fluid and a dose of DHM before bed. The criticisms are real too: the DHM amount is modest and often unclear, there's no published trial of the drink, and the price per night is high compared with plain DHM.

If you buy it, buy it for convenience, take it before bed rather than the morning after, drink water with it, and keep your expectations realistic. If you mainly want to know whether DHM helps you, start with a clearly dosed DHM product, follow the timing in our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025), and compare honestly across a few similar nights.

And whichever product you choose, the most reliable hangover prevention is still the least exciting: fewer drinks, more water, food beforehand, and a full night's sleep.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Morning Recovery actually work?**

It may help some people somewhat, but there's no published, peer-reviewed clinical trial of Morning Recovery itself. Its main active ingredient, DHM, has promising research, mostly in animals, with limited human data. Users report mixed results: some feel clearer after moderate nights, others notice little difference, especially after heavy drinking. It won't cancel out a big night.

**How much DHM is in Morning Recovery?**

It depends on the version, and many labels haven't made it easy to tell. Several versions list DHM or Hovenia dulcis extract inside a blend rather than giving a clear milligram amount of pure DHM. Independent estimates generally put it at a few hundred milligrams at most, which is lower than the 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving in many single-ingredient DHM capsules. Check the current label for the version you're buying.

**When should I drink Morning Recovery?**

During drinking or before you go to sleep, not the next morning. DHM is thought to work while your body is still processing alcohol, so taking it after the alcohol has cleared gives it much less to do. Drink some water with it as well.

**What are the side effects of Morning Recovery?**

Most people tolerate it well. The most common complaints are taste and mild stomach upset. The original formula contains sugar. DHM hasn't been studied in long-term human safety trials and may interact with sedatives and some medicines processed by the liver, so check with a doctor or pharmacist if you take prescription medicines, have liver or kidney disease, or are pregnant or breastfeeding.

**Is Morning Recovery better than DHM pills?**

Not in terms of DHM dose or value. Plain DHM capsules usually deliver more DHM per serving at a much lower cost per milligram. Morning Recovery's advantages are convenience, the drink format, and the added fluid and electrolytes, which you can also get cheaply from water and an oral rehydration packet.

**Was Morning Recovery developed in a university lab?**

The DHM research it relies on came from university labs, most notably Jing Liang's group (formerly UCLA, now USC), including a 2012 study in rats published in the Journal of Neuroscience. That research studied DHM itself, not Morning Recovery. Charles Lieber's pioneering work on how the liver processes alcohol is important background science, but we found no evidence that he or his lab developed or tested this product.

**Can I drive after drinking Morning Recovery?**

No. Morning Recovery and DHM do not make you sober and should never be used as a reason to drive after drinking. Only time lowers your blood alcohol.

**Is Morning Recovery safe to take every time I drink?**

For occasional use, most healthy adults are unlikely to have problems, but there's no long-term safety data for DHM in humans. If you're drinking often enough to want a hangover product regularly, that's worth talking over with a doctor, both for your liver and because frequent hangovers are a sign of drinking more than your body handles well.
